lead.headline: A Warm Pacific Is Quieting the Atlantic Hurricane Season
lead.deck: Forecasters say this year’s Atlantic season is likely to be a quiet one.
body: Hurricanes are giant storms that form over warm ocean water. This year, forecasters expect El Niño, a warm pattern in the Pacific Ocean. NOAA, the US weather agency, said there was a 90% chance of a strong or very strong El Niño during August, September and October.

El Niño changes the winds high in the sky over the Atlantic Ocean. Those winds can break up storms before they grow. NOAA said every strong El Niño since 1950 has come with a below-normal Atlantic hurricane season.

In August, NOAA said the chance of a below-normal season was 75%. In May, it had been 55%. It expects 7 to 13 named storms. Even so, NOAA’s leader warned that “it only takes one” storm to cause trouble.

chart.title: CHANCE OF A QUIET SEASON
chart.subtitle: NOAA forecast, percent
chart.caption: NOAA raised the chance of a below-normal season.

lead.why: Knowing a season may be quiet helps people plan, but one storm can still be dangerous, so families should keep their plans ready.

sources.title: NOAA lowers 2026 hurricane season forecast as strong El Niño suppresses Atlantic activity

science.headline: A New Kind of Clock Fixes Itself
science.deck: Scientists in Vienna ran a nuclear clock for over a day without any help.
body: A clock needs something that ticks at a steady speed. This new clock uses the nucleus of an atom of thorium-229. The nucleus is the tiny centre of an atom. A laser shines on a crystal that holds the thorium.

The big news is that the clock corrects itself. The system notices when the laser drifts and fixes it. The prototype ran for over 24 hours with no one adjusting it. It was built at TU Wien in Austria with a lab in Germany called PTB.

It is very precise. Its error is about one second in 30 million years. A long life lasts about 100 years, so it would take 300,000 of those to drift by a second. The best clocks that use whole atoms are still more precise.

illustration.title: A CLOCK THAT FIXES ITSELF
illustration.subtitle: Vienna, Austria
illustration.caption: A laser and a crystal keep the time.

science.why: Better clocks help scientists measure things very exactly, such as how fast time passes.

world.kicker: AROUND THE WORLD  •  FIJI AND TUVALU
world.headline: Island Nations Meet to Plan for a Big Climate Summit
world.deck: Leaders from the Pacific talked about keeping the planet from warming too much.
body: Fiji and Tuvalu are island nations in the Pacific Ocean. From October 5 to 8, official meetings were held in Nadi, Fiji, to get ready for COP31. COP31 is a big United Nations climate meeting. It will be held in Antalya, Türkiye, from November 9 to 20.
Tuvalu’s representative warned that the 1.5-degree goal, a limit on how much the planet warms, is in danger.

The next big step comes in Antalya, Türkiye, from November 9 to 20. That is when the COP31 summit itself takes place. Leaders from many countries will be there. Island nations like Fiji and Tuvalu want to be heard when they arrive.

challenge.title: Count a Minute
body: You need a timer or a clock with a second hand. Tap a pencil on the table at a steady speed for one minute. Ask a friend to count your taps.

Now do it again. Were both counts the same? A good clock ticks at the same speed every time. A clock that fixes itself, like the one in Vienna, keeps its ticks steady even when something tries to change them.

did_you_know.text: The Atlantic hurricane season officially runs from June 1 to November 30, so it is still going on.

explainer.title: How does El Niño quiet hurricanes?
body: Hurricanes grow best when the winds high in the sky blow gently. Tall storm clouds can then stand straight up and spin.
During El Niño, the winds high above the Atlantic get stronger. NOAA says these stronger winds disrupt storm growth, like a gust that knocks over a tower of blocks.
